title: Area X review: Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
intro: These questions mix the nine Tasks of Area X: slow flight, the Task B demonstration, power-off, power-on and accelerated stalls, the cross-controlled, elevator trim and secondary stall demonstrations, and spins. Many join two of them in one lesson flight, such as slow flight into a power-on stall, a power-off stall that turns into an elevator trim stall on the climb-out, or a cross-controlled stall that starts to spin.

questions.q: Last week you flew the Task B demonstration with a commercial learner, holding the edge of the stall and calling the horn out loud. Today, in calm air, he flies slow flight at a speed where the horn chirps on and off, says 'horn acknowledged' each time, and holds altitude within 30 feet. How do you grade it, and what is the fix?
options: Satisfactory: the CFI ACS lets a momentary warning go unpenalized, and calling it out each time is exactly the recognition that its Appendix 3 note asks for in this Task
Satisfactory: the slow flight altitude tolerance is ±100 feet, the same as in Task B, so a 30-foot hold with the warning called out meets both standards
Not to the standard: slow flight is flown with no stall warning, so lower the nose slightly and add power until it stops; holding the warning on purpose belongs only to the briefed Task B stop
Not to the standard, but only because the horn must sound steadily, not chirp; AC 61-67C has the learner hold heading and altitude with the warning device on
questions.why: Slow flight is now flown at a speed where the airplane is controllable without activating the stall warning, and any warning is corrected promptly [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]; the ACS says the same: "without a stall warning" (AI.X.A.S4), with altitude ±50 feet (AI.X.A.S5). The AFH way to find that speed is to slow to the warning, lower the nose slightly, add power and note the airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. In Task B the warning is held on purpose and acknowledged aloud at the edge (AI.X.B.S4d), with ±100 feet (AI.X.B.S1), which is why the habit must be briefed as belonging to that stop only; failure to respond to a stall warning is a listed slow flight error [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. The Appendix 3 note excuses a momentary warning caused by turbulence that is promptly corrected, not a calm-air warning left on. AC 61-67C's 'warning device activated' line is the older practice [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200a(2)]].

questions.q: Your trainer's 1G stall speed in the landing configuration is 48 knots. Your learner picks a slow flight target of 53 knots from the AFH's 5 to 10 knot guide, and in calm air the horn chirps at that speed. What do you explain, and how should the target be set?
options: The horn is out of rigging, because the rule requires the warning to stay quiet until 5 knots above the stall; write it up, and keep flying the 53-knot target until it is repaired
Keep 53 knots and call the horn out every time it sounds, because the CFI ACS accepts a stall warning in slow flight as long as the pilot acknowledges it out loud
Always fly 58 knots, the top of the AFH guide, in every configuration, because the AFH fixes slow flight at 10 knots above the 1G stall speed whatever the warning does
Many devices sound 4 to 8 knots before the stall, so up to 56 knots here; find the target by slowing to the warning, lowering the nose slightly, adding power and noting the speed
questions.why: Many stall warning devices alert 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]: 48 + 8 = 56 knots, so a 53-knot target sits inside the warning range. The AFH 5 to 10 knot figure is only a good target, and its method is to slow to the warning in the desired configuration, lower the nose slightly to stop it, add power to hold altitude and note the speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. The certification rule asks for a clear warning with sufficient margin and gives no number [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150(a)]], so the horn is not 'out of rigging'. Calling it out does not help: the slow flight standard is no stall warning (AI.X.A.S4). And the AFH sets no fixed speed for every configuration; the ACS speed is the one where any more AOA, load factor or power reduction would bring the warning (AI.X.A.S3).

questions.q: On a go-around from a balked landing with full flaps, your learner adds full power and pulls the nose up at once to climb out of ground effect, barely above the stall speed. The airplane will not climb and the horn sounds. Which slow flight idea explains it, and what is the way out?
options: Reversed command: on the back side of the power curve even full power may not give a climb; lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed, accepting a little altitude, then climb and raise the flaps in small increments
Speed stability above L/DMAX: hold the attitude and wait, because the airspeed comes back by itself once the airplane is out of ground effect and the induced drag falls away
Not enough lift: the throttle is already full, so raise the nose and trim further nose-up, since a higher AOA always gives more lift and therefore a better climb at any airspeed
Adverse yaw from the flaps: level the wings with rudder alone and hold the pitch, because the horn is reacting to the sideslip from the flaps and not to the angle of attack
questions.why: The PHAK's reversed command examples are exactly this: climbing out of ground effect too slowly can leave the airplane unable to climb even at full power, and the only recourse is to lower the pitch and accept some altitude loss [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. The AFH go-around text says an airplane cannot climb below minimum power required speed, the pilot should resist any impulse to pitch up when the airspeed is insufficient, and it may be right to lower the nose briefly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; climbing prematurely out of ground effect is a listed go-around error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]], and the flaps come up in small increments [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The speed instability that keeps a slow airplane decaying applies below L/DMAX, not above it [[24:115|AFH 5-10]], so waiting does not fix it. More nose-up only adds drag on the back side [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

questions.q: Building the Task B ground brief, your learner marks 'reversed command starts here' at best glide speed (L/DMAX) on the power-required curve. Where do the CFI ACS and the PHAK put that line?
options: At L/DMAX, as she drew it, because minimum drag and minimum power required always fall at the same airspeed, so best glide is where more power first becomes necessary
At the minimum power required speed, the curve's lowest point, which the PHAK calls maximum endurance; minimum drag (L/DMAX) is a different point
At the bottom of the green arc (VS1), because reversed command is defined by the stall speed marking, and every speed above VS1 is in the region of normal command
At design maneuvering speed (VA), the S4a stop, because above VA more speed needs more power and below VA less speed needs more power to hold the altitude
questions.why: The ACS names the minimum power required speed and "its role in differentiating the region of normal command and the region of reversed command" (AI.X.B.K3). The PHAK puts reversed command below the speed for maximum endurance, the lowest point on the power curve [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]], and says the minimum power and maximum endurance point is a different point from minimum drag [[1:105|PHAK 5-8]]. Best glide occurs at L/DMAX [[24:83|AFH 3-22]], so it is not the line, even though the AFH slow flight text uses L/DMAX as a shorthand [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]; the AFH's own Figure 4-4 divides the curve at the minimum power airspeed [[24:91|AFH 4-5]]. VS1 and VA are airspeed limits, not points that divide the power curve.

questions.q: During the clean Task B demonstration your learner asks to see how much extra power a bank costs. You could show it with a level 20° turn at the S4a, S4b or S4c stop. Which do you pick, and why?
options: S4c, the edge of the stall, because the power-required curve is steepest there, so the rise in rpm on the tachometer is largest and easiest for the learner to see and note
S4a, maneuvering speed, because any control input made at or below VA, in any number of axes at once, is structurally safe, so a brisk roll into the bank cannot hurt anything
S4b, best glide: the bank needs more AOA and power there too, and there is margin, while at the S4c airspeed any added load factor stalls the airplane
None of them, because the CFI ACS forbids any bank during Task B: its bank tolerance applies only to the landing configuration sequence, never to the clean sequence
questions.why: In a bank the load factor rises, so the pilot adds AOA, which raises induced drag and the power required at any speed [[24:92|AFH 4-6]]; the extra thrust needed grows with the bank [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]. At the S4c airspeed any further increase in AOA or load factor, or any power reduction, means an immediate stall by definition (AI.X.B.S4c), so a bank there is a stall, not a demonstration. Best glide shows the same effect with room to spare. VA protects only a single full input in one axis; it gives no protection against inputs in more than one axis at once [[1:275|PHAK 11-19]]. The ACS S1 tolerance includes the specified bank angle ±5°, as appropriate (AI.X.B.S1), so a bank is not forbidden.

questions.q: At the S5d stop, holding the edge of the stall with full flaps, your learner sees the altitude sag 40 feet and gives the yoke a quick tug to get it back. The buffet turns into a break. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: An accelerated stall from pulling too fast: at the edge any added AOA or load factor stalls at once; use small, smooth inputs, power for altitude, and reduce AOA first if it stalls
A power-off stall caused by the flaps: raise them to the takeoff setting before the S5d stop, because full flaps are only used for the acceleration in S5f, not at the edge
The right priority, badly timed: 40 feet was already past the ±100-foot tolerance for this Task, so a quick pull to win back the altitude had to come first, before power or anything else
A secondary stall, because the warning had been on too long: the fix is to trim nose-up before reaching the edge so the horn stays silent while the learner holds the stop
questions.why: S5d is the airspeed where any further increase in AOA or load factor, or reduction in power, would stall immediately (AI.X.B.S5d), so a tug there stalls the wing. 'Inadvertent accelerated stall by pulling too fast on the controls' is a listed stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], and abrupt or rough control movements in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Altitude at the edge is held with power, which is needed as the speed nears the target [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. If it stalls, the most important action is to reduce the AOA [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. A 40-foot sag is inside ±100 feet (AI.X.B.S1), and S5d is flown with gear and flaps fully extended (AI.X.B.S5d), so neither tempting excuse holds.

questions.q: In a turning power-off stall at 20° of bank, your learner jerks the yoke back 'to get it over with'. You feel seat pressure, the break comes sharply at a higher airspeed than his straight-ahead stalls, and the low wing drops. What do you name, and what fix do you give?
options: A cross-control stall from too little rudder: next time hold inside rudder through the pull, so the low wing stays up at the break and the turn stays tight
A secondary stall caused by the bank: enter every power-off stall wings level, because the CFI ACS no longer includes a turning version of this Task
Nothing to correct: the jerk only shortened the entry, and the higher break speed came from the 20° bank, which by itself raises the stall speed by about a third over wings level
An inadvertent accelerated stall from pulling too fast: raise the nose smoothly and hold the stall attitude, and at the break reduce AOA before leveling the wings
questions.why: Pulling too fast on a power-off or power-on entry is listed as an inadvertent accelerated stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]; any stall above +1G comes at a higher indicated airspeed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]], and stalls from abrupt maneuvers tend to be more aggressive [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. The AFH entry raises the nose smoothly to the stall attitude and holds it [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. At the break, aileron before AOA can deepen the stall at the tip and roll the airplane further [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. A level 20° bank adds very little: the stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]], and 1/cos 20° = 1.064, whose square root is 1.03, about 3 percent, not a third. The ACS still has turning stalls, bank not to exceed 20° ±5° (AI.X.C.S6), and inside rudder makes a skid, the cross-control setup [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

questions.q: Flying a left turning power-off stall at 15° of bank from a heading of 090, your learner plans to vary the bank so the break comes exactly on 360, 'like rolling out on a heading'. What do you teach?
options: Good plan: the ±10° heading tolerance applies to the turning stall as well, so the break must come within 10° of a heading the learner chooses before the entry
Hold a constant, coordinated 15° bank and do not try to stall on a set heading; expect the break within about 90° of turn, as in a turn from base to final
Fly it wings level instead, because the CFI ACS keeps turning stalls for the power-on Task only and uses bank only in the cross-controlled demonstration
Let the bank steepen as the speed decays, because more bank brings the stall sooner and keeps the turn inside 90°, the most heading change the ACS permits
questions.why: The AFH says no attempt should be made to stall or recover on a predetermined heading, but to simulate the base-to-final turn the stall normally should come within a heading change of about 90°; the turn continues at a constant bank, coordinated, until the stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Failure to maintain a constant bank in turning stalls is a listed error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. The ACS ±10° applies to the heading in straight flight; in turning flight the standard is the specified bank, not to exceed 20°, ±5° (AI.X.C.S6). A steepening bank in a skid can go to a dangerous attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

questions.q: You finish slow flight with a private learner at 50 knots, full flaps, holding 3,500 feet. Next is a straight-ahead power-on stall, and she says, 'We're already slow and nose-high, so I'll leave the flaps down, go to full power right here and pull.' What do you teach?
options: Set the takeoff, departure or cruise configuration, slow to lift-off speed, then set no less than 65 percent power and raise the nose smoothly
Good plan: slow flight is the ideal entry, because the AFH adds full power at the slowest speed the pilot can hold so that the stall comes with the least altitude lost
Keep the flaps down but set only 50 percent power, because the CFI ACS caps power-on stalls at half power to hold the pitch below 30° in every training airplane
Accelerate to cruise first, then pull up briskly at full power, because a power-on stall has to start from cruise speed to show the left-turning forces at their strongest
questions.why: Power-on stalls are flown in the takeoff configuration, and also clean; the pilot slows to normal lift-off speed and only then sets takeoff or climb power, to avoid an excessively steep nose-up attitude held for a long time [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The ACS asks for the takeoff, departure or cruise configuration as the evaluator specifies (AI.X.D.S3) and no less than 65 percent power (AI.X.D.S4); full flaps is the landing configuration. 65 percent is a floor, not a cap: Appendix 3 lets some high-performance airplanes use less only to keep the pitch at or below 30°. Then the nose comes up smoothly, since pulling too fast on a power-on entry is the accelerated stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

questions.q: In slow flight at low power your learner held the ball centered with a modest push on the right pedal. Now, in a takeoff-configuration power-on stall at full power, the ball drifts right and the nose slides left as the nose comes up. He says, 'I'm holding the same right rudder as in slow flight.' What do you tell him?
options: That is enough: once climb power is set the left-turning forces stay constant, so a ball slightly right is normal and the stall recovery will center it again
Use left aileron instead of more rudder, because P-factor is a rolling force, and the ailerons are the control that balances it at high power and low airspeed
Reduce the power below 65 percent so the slow flight rudder is enough, because the CFI ACS lets the instructor choose any power that keeps the ball centered
Add right rudder progressively as the speed decays, all the way to the stall: at full power and high AOA the slipstream and P-factor yaw grow
questions.why: In the power-on stall entry, as the airspeed decreases the pilot moves the elevator progressively back while adding right rudder, all the way to the full stall [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. The AFH slow flight text says the same thing in general: the closer to the stall and the higher the power, the more right rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. The PHAK ties the corkscrew slipstream to high propeller speed and low forward speed, as in power-on stall approaches [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]], and P-factor to a high AOA [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]], so the forces are not constant. Allowing the airplane to yaw is a listed climb error [[24:81|AFH 3-20]], and yaw at the stall is what starts a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. The ACS power floor is 65 percent (AI.X.D.S4).

questions.q: In a clean power-on stall at full power, your learner notices the break came below the bottom of the green arc and decides the airspeed indicator must be faulty. What do you explain?
options: The indicator is faulty: installation error is greatest at high power settings, so any stall that breaks below the green arc means a pitot or static problem to write up
Same critical AOA: the arc marks a power-off stall speed, and power lowers the stall speed, as in the PHAK sample table (clean, wings level: 54 knots power on, 65 off)
The nose was much higher, so the wing reached a higher AOA than in a power-off stall, and a higher stalling AOA always gives a lower stalling airspeed with the power on
The airplane was lighter than the arc assumes, and weight is the only factor that moves the stall below the green arc, since power does not change the stall speed at all
questions.why: A given airplane always stalls at the same AOA, whatever its airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. VS1, the bottom of the green arc, is usually the power-off stall speed at maximum takeoff weight, clean [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. In the PHAK sample table, gear and flaps up, wings level, the stall is 54 knots power on and 65 knots power off [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. Airspeed indicator errors are generally greatest at low airspeeds, not at high power [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. Weight does move the stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]], but it is not the only factor, so the 'weight only' answer fails too.

questions.q: For a power-on accelerated stall your learner levels at the briefed VA for today's weight, leaves climb power in and rolls into a coordinated 45° bank. As he starts the pull, the airspeed is climbing past VA. What do you teach?
options: Pull harder and sooner, because a firmer pull bleeds off the extra speed quickly, and the VA limit applies to the roll-in, not to the pull that follows it
Carry on, because the VA limit in the ACS applies only to the power-off version, and the power-on version stalls at a lower indicated airspeed anyway
Stop the pull, reduce power and let the speed settle at or below VA before adding back pressure, so the wing stalls before it can be overstressed
Extend partial flaps to slow down, because flaps add drag and also lower the stall speed, which keeps the break well below VA during the steep turn
questions.why: The ACS asks for power set so the airspeed does not exceed VA or any other POH/AFM limit (AI.X.E.S4), and the AFH says never above the manufacturer's speed, VA or VO [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. At or below VA the wing reaches the critical AOA, which unloads it, before the design load limit; above VA it can reach the limit load first, so more pull can overstress the airplane [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. A harder pull above VA is exactly that case: stalled at 1.7 times the normal stall speed, the load factor is about 2.89 G [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Flaps are never used for accelerated stalls because the design G limits are lower with them out [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

questions.q: On his first accelerated stall your learner holds a coordinated 45° bank and firms up the pull. The buffet starts with the nose only a little above the horizon, and he keeps pulling: 'The nose isn't high yet, so it can't be the stall.' What do you teach?
options: This stall can come at a lower pitch attitude and a higher airspeed than he expects, and attitude is never a sure cue; in this Task the recovery starts at the first indication
He is right to wait: buffet in a steep turn is only the load factor, and the wing cannot stall until the nose reaches the same pitch as in his 1G stalls
Keep pulling until the horn sounds, because the evaluator chooses a full stall for this Task, and the horn is the first indication of a stall that the ACS names
Shallow the bank to 30° before calling the stall, so the nose can rise higher and he can see the stall picture he has already learned from his 1G stalls
questions.why: The AFH warns that stalls from abrupt maneuvers occur at higher-than-normal airspeeds or at lower-than-anticipated pitch attitudes, so they can surprise an inexperienced pilot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], and vision is not a foolproof stall cue [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. ACS S6 asks for the cues to be acknowledged at the first indication of a stall, such as buffet or the horn (AI.X.E.S6), and Appendix 3 says this Task recovers at the first indication; the evaluator does not ask for a full stall here. The longer it takes to recognize an impending stall, the more likely a full stall [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Changing the bank does not change the wing's critical AOA [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

questions.q: One lesson flight with a CFI applicant: power-off stalls, then the cross-controlled stall demonstration, then spins. The highest terrain in the practice area is 1,400 feet MSL. Under the CFI ACS, what is the lowest MSL altitude at which each Task may be completed?
options: 2900 feet for all three, because the AFH 1,500-foot AGL recovery floor applies to every stall and to every intentional spin
4400 feet for all three, because any stall flown on a lesson that also includes spins takes the 3,000-foot floor of the spin Task
2900 feet for the power-off stalls, 4400 feet for the cross-controlled stall and 4900 feet for the spins
2900 feet for the power-off stalls, 4400 feet for the cross-controlled stall and 5400 feet for the spins
questions.why: Each Task has its own S2 floor: power-off stalls no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (AI.X.C.S2), the cross-controlled stall no lower than 3,000 feet AGL (AI.X.F.S2) and spins no lower than 4,000 feet AGL (AI.X.I.S2). With terrain at 1,400 feet: 1,400 + 1,500 = 2,900; 1,400 + 3,000 = 4,400; 1,400 + 4,000 = 5,400 feet MSL. These are completion floors, so each entry must be higher by the airplane's own altitude loss. The AFH 1,500-foot AGL figures [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] and AC 61-67C's 'above 3,500 feet AGL' for spin training [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300b]] (which gives 4,900) are not the checkride numbers, and spins carry 4,000 feet, not 3,000.

questions.q: On a hot afternoon at a high-elevation airport, your learner keeps overshooting the turn to final at her usual 25° bank, and starts adding inside rudder to swing the nose around. The indicated speeds are the same as at home. What do you explain?
options: Density altitude raises the indicated stall speed, so she should fly faster on base and tighten the turn with rudder, which is safe once she is above that higher stall speed
The same indicated speed is a higher true airspeed here, so the turn radius at a given bank is larger; plan the base for it, keep the bank at or below 30° and go around rather than skid
Nothing has changed at the same indicated speed, so the overshoot is a wind problem only, and a little inside rudder is acceptable while the ball stays within one ball width
Steepen the bank to 45° for every turn to final at high airports, because the extra load factor is offset by the higher true airspeed that the thinner air gives the airplane
questions.why: Altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed, but thinner air gives a higher true airspeed for the same indicated airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]], and at a given bank a higher airspeed makes the turn radius larger [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. That sets up the AFH overshoot: the pilot steepens the bank, pulls and adds inside rudder, the bank increases, the nose slices down and a stall with those inputs may rapidly become a spin. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; low in the pattern, be reluctant to bank more than 30° and do not skid [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Inside rudder is the skid itself, and a 45° bank is the steep turn the AFH warns against at that height.

questions.q: You set up a full-flap power-off stall from a trimmed approach glide, as on short final. At the break your learner pushes, then adds full power and relaxes the push 'to let it climb'. The nose rises well past the climb picture and swings left, and the horn comes back. What is he showing you, and what do you teach?
options: A power-off stall that never ended: he should pull the throttle back to idle and repeat the full recovery, since full power cannot be used until the flaps are fully retracted
Normal behavior at full power with full flaps: let the nose rise and add a little back pressure, because the climb attitude keeps the airspeed from going past the top of the white arc
The elevator trim stall setup: approach trim plus propwash raise the nose; hold considerable forward pressure and right rudder, then trim nose-down and raise the flaps in steps
A cross-control stall caused by the left swing: hold left aileron against the yaw and keep the rudder neutral until the wings are level, then trim and raise the flaps all at once
questions.why: With the trim set for an approach glide, the combined effects of propwash over the tail and the trim make the nose rise sharply and turn left, and at full throttle the pitch goes above the normal climbing attitude [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. The AFH go-around guidance: expect considerable forward elevator pressure, use right rudder for torque and P-factor, rough trim once the attitude and airspeed are right, and retract the flaps in small increments [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. After a simulated approach stall the climb is established as in a go-around [[24:122|AFH 5-17]], so this is exactly the real-world link. Cutting the power is wrong: power reduces altitude loss in a recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Letting the nose rise with the speed low invites a secondary stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

questions.q: Practicing go-arounds at altitude from a full-flap glide, your learner's callout is 'Flaps up, pitch up, power.' On the next one he raises all the flaps, pitches up, the airplane settles and the horn sounds before the power is in. What order do you teach, and why?
options: Power, attitude, configuration: full power smoothly first, then forward pressure and right rudder for a safe attitude, then the flaps up in small increments
Pitch, power, flaps: set the attitude first so the airspeed is protected, then add full power, then raise all the flaps at once so the drag goes away as quickly as possible
Flaps, power, pitch: drag is the main enemy at low speed, so raising the flaps first is right, and his only mistake was pitching up for the climb before the power was in
Power, flaps, attitude: full power first, then all the flaps up at once to stop any ballooning, and only then raise the nose, since the trim will hold it during the cleanup
questions.why: The AFH gives three cardinal principles in order: power, attitude, configuration. Full or maximum allowable power goes in smoothly and without hesitation; the pilot resists any pitch-up while the airspeed is insufficient, expects considerable forward pressure and uses right rudder; and the flaps come up in small increments, because a sudden, complete retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. AC 61-67C shows the secondary stall link: retracting the flaps rapidly while holding a higher than normal climb pitch can give a secondary stall or settling with altitude loss [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]]. Improper pitch attitude is a listed go-around error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

questions.q: In the preflight briefing you plan to show the secondary stall by recovering from a full stall and then pulling the nose up abruptly before flying speed returns. The evaluator says to use full flaps. What do the sources lead you to say?
options: Full flaps make the abrupt pull safer, because the flaps lower the stall speed, so the second stall comes at a lower airspeed and puts a smaller load on the airplane
An abrupt pull-up stall is an accelerated stall, never practiced with flaps out; fly that version clean, and show a flaps-down second stall with a too-high climb pitch
The ACS lets the evaluator pick the configuration, so fly the abrupt pull with full flaps and pull harder than usual, since the flaps raise the G limits of the airplane
Decline the Task, because secondary stalls may only be shown clean, and the AC 61-67C go-around exercise with flaps out is a power-on stall, not a secondary stall
questions.why: The AFH calls any stall above +1G, such as one from pulling up, an accelerated stall, and says a pilot should never practice accelerated stalls with the flaps extended because of the lower design G-load limits in that configuration [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The ACS asks for a stall in a specified configuration and a second exceedance of the critical AOA (AI.X.H.S3), so the configuration should be agreed in the briefing. AC 61-67C's exercise gives the flaps-down version: after a full-flap stall, attempting to climb with the flaps extended at a higher than normal pitch gives a secondary stall [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]]. Flaps lower the G limits; they do not raise them.

questions.q: In your clean secondary stall demonstration, the second break leaves the nose well down and the airspeed passing 90 knots and rising. Your learner, following along, asks why you are not hauling the nose up now to save altitude, or else holding the dive until near the red line to be sure the wing is flying. What do you explain?
options: Haul it up now: after two stalls altitude is what is scarce, and the wing cannot stall again while the airspeed indicator reads above the published stall speed
Hold the dive to near the red line: speed in hand is the only protection against another break in the pull-out, because no stall can happen at any speed above VA
Add full power and hold the attitude until the speed stops rising, then trim nose-up and let the airplane level itself, so no pull is needed in the recovery at all
Neither: dive only to about cruising or maneuvering speed, then pull up gradually once safely above the stall, about 2 to 2.5 G; a hard pull invites a third stall, a long dive excess speed
questions.why: The PHAK says a stall recovery made by diving only to cruising or design maneuvering speed, with a gradual pull-up as soon as the airspeed is safely above stalling, can be done at no more than 2 or 2.5 G, and that abrupt pull-ups may produce recurrent or secondary stalls [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. The critical AOA can be exceeded at any airspeed [[24:117|AFH 5-12]], so the published stall speed is no shield in a hard pull. Inadvertent secondary stall and excessive airspeed buildup are both listed errors [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], and the airspeed must never reach the red line in a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]. Full power in a steep dive only builds speed faster.

questions.q: Your right-turn cross-controlled stall demonstration in a spin-approved trainer goes too far and the airplane starts to rotate. Your applicant, following along, sees the ball pinned to the left and calls 'left spin, right rudder', but the turn coordinator's symbolic airplane is banked right. What do you teach?
options: Trust the turn coordinator: it is a right spin, so full left rudder; in a spin the ball moves with its mounting location and can sit left even in a right spin
Trust the ball, since in a spin it always moves toward the low wing; the turn coordinator's gyro tumbles in rotation and shows nothing useful until the spin stops
Call it a left spin, because a spin from crossed controls always rotates toward the raised wing, and in a right turn the raised wing is the left one
Neither instrument helps, so neutralize the rudder and push the stick forward, since the direction stops mattering once forward elevator lowers the AOA
questions.why: The AFH says the turn indicator's symbolic airplane shows the spin direction, the ball should not be used, and a ball mounted on the left side always moves left, even in a spin to the right [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. A stall in a skidding turn can spin in the direction of the rudder, regardless of which wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]; here the right rudder of the right-turn skid agrees with the turn coordinator. Recovery uses full rudder opposite the rotation, applied briskly and held, and rudder tends to be the most important control [[24:130|AFH 5-25]], so the direction matters. Start incipient spin recovery before 360° of rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

questions.q: A commercial pilot applicant you are training asks you to add three spins to tomorrow's lesson in your spin-approved trainer 'to be a safer pilot'. You have no parachutes on board. Under 14 CFR 91.307, what applies?
options: No parachutes are needed, because 91.307(d) exempts any spin given by a certificated flight instructor, whatever certificate or rating the pilot is training for
No parachutes are needed, because the commercial ACS includes spin awareness, so spins count as maneuvers required by the regulations for that certificate
Spins are required for the flight instructor rating, not the commercial, so the 91.307(d) exception does not fit; 91.307(c) governs, and spins need approved parachutes for each occupant
Only you need a parachute, because in spin training the instructor giving it must wear one while the pilot receiving it is exempt
questions.why: Under 91.307(c), unless each occupant wears an approved parachute, no pilot carrying any person other than a crewmember may make an intentional maneuver past 60° of bank or 30° nose-up or nose-down. Paragraph (d) lifts that only for flight tests for a certificate or rating, and for spins and other maneuvers required by the regulations for a certificate or rating when given by a CFI (or an ATP under 61.67) [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]]. Part 61 training does not include actual spins for anyone other than flight instructor airplane and glider applicants [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]], so this ride fits neither part of (d). In required CFI spin training neither the person receiving the instruction nor the instructor must wear one [[13:20|AC 61-67C 301b]], so the 'instructor only' answer is wrong too.

questions.q: The evaluator, playing your learner, enters a spin with full rudder but lets the elevator come only halfway back. The nose drops steeply and the airspeed rises through 100 knots and keeps climbing. Which error do you name, and which recovery fits?
options: A fully developed spin with a fast rotation: power to idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, then brisk forward elevator held until the airspeed stops rising
Recovery rudder that was not brisk enough: hold full opposite rudder longer and pull firmly, because the rising airspeed shows the wing is no longer stalled
An accelerated spin caused by power: leave the rudder in, close the throttle and wait, because a trainer recovers on its own within half a turn once the power is off
Not holding full up-elevator on entry, giving a spiral, not a spin: idle, unload to about 1 G, roll level with coordinated controls, then raise the nose gently
questions.why: 'Failure to apply and maintain full up-elevator pressure during spin entry, resulting in a spiral' is the second AFH spin error, and its spiral recovery is: power to idle, some forward elevator to unload to about +1G, roll wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder, then gently raise the nose and climb only once the speed is safe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. If the airspeed is increasing, the airplane is no longer in a spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]; AC 61-67C also tells you to recognize the spiral by rapidly increasing airspeed and recover at once [[13:20|AC 61-67C 300f]]. Spin recovery inputs treat a stall that is no longer there, and pulling back rapidly while rolling level is the reaction the AFH says can create loads that damage the airframe [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

questions.q: Your applicant learned on power-off stalls never to pick up a dropping wing with aileron before the AOA is reduced. In her first spin recovery she neutralizes the ailerons, then, as the rotation slows, adds aileron against the rotation 'to help level the wings sooner'. What do you teach?
options: Good technique: aileron against the rotation works like extra opposite rudder and shortens the recovery, as long as the forward elevator is already in
Keep the ailerons neutral: aileron against the spin can flatten it and may even make it unrecoverable, and aileron with the spin can speed the rotation
Use aileron with the rotation instead, because that lowers the AOA on the descending wing and so stops the autorotation sooner than the rudder alone
The ailerons do not matter in a spin, because the whole wing is stalled and they have no effect at all; only the rudder and elevator change the recovery
questions.why: Step 2 of the AFH spin recovery is ailerons neutral: aileron in the direction of the spin may speed the rotation, steepen the attitude and delay the recovery, and aileron opposite the spin may flatten the spin, delay the recovery or even cause an unrecoverable spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. AC 61-67C also has the pilot neutralize the ailerons [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]], and the manufacturer's procedure comes first [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Her stall habit points the same way: aileron used before the AOA is reduced can deepen the stall at the tip [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. The ailerons are not without effect; that is why the AFH warns about them.
